Logic cells are like those in your processor, and in that form, they're all the same sort of thing: switching transistors. DRAM is different because each cell is made up of a transistor and a capacitor, and that complicates scaling. For a long time now, we've been making those cells with a geometry known as "6F²", and the 'holy grail' was the ultimate move to 4F², offering a theoretical 33% density improvement. Now, Micron says that despite putting "over two decades" of research into the idea, it's throwing in the towel and sticking to 6F² for the foreseeable future. This might seem absurd, but you have to understand that these are cell geometries, not process nodes. In essence, these terms describe the shape and layout of the DRAM cell, not its physical size directly; that is determined by the combination of layout and process node. DRAM doesn't use the same node nomenclature as logic; because of the mixed cell type (transistors and capacitors), it doesn't scale the same way; to mark node changes, DRAM vendors currently use terminology like "1γ" and "1δ"—those being the Greek letters gamma and delta, used in this case to signify serial improvements over time. (Btw, I heard that the cool kids are calling this a Meat Proxy.) But anyway, the reason I decided to post about this is that Emily has a very simple framework that she uses for working with AI, which she calls the “Brain Sandwich”, that solves this. It’s both about taking full advantage of AI without letting your engineering skills atrophy. The idea is very simple, and can be summarized by: whenever you work on something, you should use: Your brain, and then AI, and then Your brain Explaining a bit more… Before you tell the agent to start building anything, you go there and read and understand it first. You don’t need a complete implementation plan, but you need a rough idea of where you’re going. Otherwise, AI can bias you in the wrong direction. Or even worse, it can nudge you into building something that wasn’t even a problem you needed to solve in the first place! Now that you have all this context, that’s the time to bring AI. By all means, do it. Fully delegate this part with no shame! And when the agent brings you the solution, you will know if it’s right, or if it’s too much, or if it’s completely solving the wrong problem, etc. Then, at the end, your brain comes back. Because before sending your stuff to other people for review, you need to make the work reviewable. Read the diff, check if the complexity is worth it in this case, improve the freaking PR description, etc. The rule of thumb is: if you can’t explain what’s changing and why, it’s not ready for someone else to take a look. The security issue is tracked as CVE-2026-111497 and is also known as “Broccoli2Shell” and “Node2Shell.” It affects Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.0.9, 1.1.0, and 1.2.0. The vulnerability has been reported under several names because it was initially identified in Node.js before researchers found that the same flaw in the Brotli decoder could affect software across multiple ecosystems. Brotli is an open-source project developed and maintained by Google for lossless data compression. It shrinks files so they can be transmitted faster without affecting the original data. Broad impact The name HTTP2Shell reflects its impact on HTTP clients and servers, although the vulnerability is not specific to HTTP/2 and can affect other applications that decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data. Apart from Node.js, potentially affected software includes Python HTTP clients such as urllib3[brotli], requests, httpx, and aiohttp[speedups], when configured with a vulnerable Brotli decoder, as well as other applications and tools that use vulnerable Brotli implementations. On Sunday, Microsoft pushed an emergency security update to address the issue in .NET, warning that successful exploitation allows privilege escalation on systems with a vulnerable .NET version. homepage.title: LEANN: A Low-Storage Vector Index
homepage.description: Embedding-based vector search underpins many important applications, such as recommendation and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). It relies on vector indices to enable efficient search. However, these indices require storing high-dimensional embeddings and large index metadata, whose total size can be several times larger than the original data (e.g., text chunks). Such high storage overhead makes it difficult, or even impractical, to deploy vector search on personal devices or large-scale datasets. To tackle this problem, we propose LEANN, a storage-efficient index for vector search that recomputes embeddings on the fly instead of storing them, and compresses state-of-the-art proximity graph indices while preserving search accuracy. LEANN delivers high-quality vector search while using only a fraction of the storage (e.g., 5% of the original data) and supporting storage-efficient index construction and updates. On real-world benchmarks, LEANN reduces index size by up to 50x compared with conventional indices, while maintaining SOTA accuracy and comparable latency for RAG applications.

Closing thoughts Share this article Elixir Popcorn 1.0: Moving from AtomVM to OTP/BEAM Kuba Gonet • Oct 27, 2026 • 9 min read Popcorn is a library that lets you run Elixir in the browser. We recently released Popcorn 1.0, which replaces AtomVM with OTP/BEAM as the underlying VM and marks it as a first stable release. For browser applications built with Popcorn, this gives much broader OTP compatibility, makes it much harder to crash or hang Popcorn's VM, and creates a stable foundation for future releases. I want to take a moment to talk about the whys and hows. Why we moved away from AtomVM Popcorn started as a research project. We wanted to see how far we could take the "Elixir on the web" idea, and where it would break down. We took it surprisingly far, considering that the Wasm ecosystem is still developing. We decided to run a real VM in the browser. Compared to other approaches (compiling .beam files to Wasm or Elixir AST to JS), this has the upside of supporting Elixir semantics closely. We used AtomVM as the underlying runtime. It's a small VM aimed at embedded uses, implementing a subset of OTP/BEAM. At the time, it seemed like a perfect fit for browsers, which in some ways resemble embedded targets; the VM itself is small, hackable, and frankly, it was enjoyable to work on its code. We also didn't think the BEAM could be compiled to Wasm. It's quite a complex project with a long history. It isn't optimized for binary size and browser speed. Additionally, we saw some previous attempts to compile it for browser use, and they didn't look promising.
